cab.g: A compartment at the front of a truck or train for the driver.
A former Hebrew unit of volume, about equal to 1.3 L as a dry measure or 1.25 L as a liquid measure.

cabin.e: From Middle English caban, cabane, from Old French cabane, from Medieval Latin capanna (“a cabin”); see further etymology there.
cabin.g: A small dwelling characteristic of the frontier, especially when built from logs with simple tools and not constructed by professional build

cage.e: From Middle English cage, from Old French cage, from Latin cavea.
cage.g: An enclosure made of spaced bars, normally to hold animals while providing some ventilation.

cake.e: From Middle English cake, from Old Norse kaka (“cake”) (compare Norwegian kake, Icelandic/Swedish kaka, Danish kage), from Proto-Germanic *kakǭ, of disputed origin. Likely a distant cognate with kaak. Perhaps related to cookie, kuchen, and quiche.
cake.g: A rich, sweet dessert food, typically made of flour, sugar, and eggs and baked in an oven, and often covered in icing.

calamity.e: From Middle French calamité, from Latin calamitās (“loss, damage; disaster”).
calamity.g: An event resulting in great loss.

calculate.e: Borrowed from Latin calculātus, perfect passive participle of calculō (“to reckon, compute, calculate”, originally by means of pebbles) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from calculus (“a pebble”), further from calx (“limestone”, calc- in compounds) + -ulus (forms diminutives).
calculate.g: To determine the value of something or the solution to something by a mathematical process.

calf.e: From Middle English calf, from Anglian Old English cælf, calf (West Saxon ċealf), from Proto-West Germanic *kalb, from Proto-Germanic *kalbaz, further etymology unknown.
calf.g: A young cow or bull of any bovid, such as domestic cattle or buffalo.

calf.e: From Middle English calf, kalf, from Old Norse kalfi, possibly derived from the same Germanic root as English calf (“young cow”) (above).
calf.g: The back of the leg below the knee.

call.e: From Middle English callen, from Old English ċeallian (“to call, shout”) and Old Norse kalla (“to call; shout; refer to as; name”); both from Proto-Germanic *kalzōną (“to call, shout”), from Proto-Indo-European *golH-so- (“voice, cry”), from *gel(H)- (“to vocalize, call, shout”).
call.g: To reach out with one's voice.

calling.e: From Middle English callyng, kallyng, kalland, from Old English *cealliende and Old Norse kallandi, equivalent to call + -ing.

callous.e: From Latin callōsus (“hard-skinned”), from callum (“hardened skin”) + -ōsus.
callous.g: Emotionally hardened; unfeeling and indifferent to the suffering/feelings of others.

calm.e: From Middle English calm, calme, from Middle French calme, probably from Old Italian calma, of uncertain origin. Calma may derive from Late Latin cauma (“heat of the midday sun”), from Ancient Greek καῦμα (kaûma, “heat, especially of the sun”), from καίω (kaíō, “to burn”), or possibly from Latin caleō.
calm.g: Peaceful, quiet, especially free from anger and anxiety.

calve.e: From Middle English calven, from Old English *calfian, cealfian, from Proto-West Germanic *kalbōn, from Proto-Germanic *kalbōną (“to calve”), from *kalbaz (“calf”).
calve.g: To give birth to a calf.

came.g: A grooved strip of metal, traditionally usually lead or brass and today sometimes stainless steel, used to hold panes of glass together in g

camel.e: From Middle English camel, through Old English camel and Old Northern French camel (Old French chamel, modern French chameau), from Latin camēlus, from Ancient Greek κάμηλος (kámēlos), from a Semitic source, ultimately from Proto-Semitic *gamal-; compare Arabic جَمَل (jamal), Hebrew גמל (gamál), Aramaic ܓܡܠܐ (gamlā), Coptic ϭⲁⲙⲟⲩⲗ (čamoul).
camel.g: A mammalian beast of burden, much used in desert areas, of the genus Camelus.

camp.e: From Middle English kampe (“battlefield, open space”), from Old English camp (“battle, contest, battlefield, open space”), from Proto-West Germanic *kamp (“open field where military exercises are held, level plain”), from Latin campus (“open field, level plain”), from Proto-Indo-European *kh₂emp- (“to bend; crooked”).
camp.g: An outdoor place acting as temporary accommodation in tents or other simple structures.

camp.e: Unknown. Suggested origins include the 17th century French word camper (“to put oneself in a pose”), an assumed dialectal English word *camp or *kemp (“rough, uncouth”) and a derivation from camp (n.) Believed to be from Polari, but otherwise obscure.
camp.g: An affected, exaggerated, or intentionally tasteless style.

campaign.e: From French campagne, from Italian campagna (“field, military operation”), from Late Latin campānia (“open country, battlefield”), from Latin campus (“field”).
campaign.g: A series of operations undertaken to achieve a set goal.

camphire.e: Malapropism in the English Bible of the Hebrew כֹּפֶר / כּוֹפֶר (kōp̄er, “henna”) by confusion with camphor. The Hebrew is from Akkadian 𒇒𒌓𒀀 (kupru, “bitumen, pitch”) from Akkadian 𒅗𒉺𒊒 (kapāru, “to smear, to daub on”).

can.e: From Middle English can, first and third person singular of connen, cunnen (“to be able, know how”), from Old English can(n), first and third person singular of cunnan (“to know how”), from Proto-West Germanic *kunnan, from Proto-Germanic *kunnaną, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵneh₃- (whence also know).
From Middle English canne, from Old English canne (“glass, container, cup, jar”), from Proto-Germanic *kannǭ (“can, tankard, mug, cup”).
can.g: A container or vessel, especially for liquids, usually made of metal.

can't.g: Cannot (negative modal auxiliary); be unable to; not have the ability to (whether due to lacking relevant strength or skill or knowledge or

canal.e: Borrowed from Middle French canal, from Old French canal, from Latin canālis (“channel, canal, narrow passage”), from canna (“reed, cane”), from Ancient Greek κάννα (kánna, “reed”), from Akkadian 𒄀 (qanû, “reed”).
canal.g: An artificial waterway or artificially improved river used for travel, shipping, or irrigation.

cancel.e: From Middle English cancellen, from Anglo-Norman canceler (“to cross out with lines”) (modern French chanceler (“to stagger, sway”)), from Old French canceler, from Latin cancellō (“to make resemble a lattice”), from cancellus (“a railing or lattice”), diminutive of cancer (“a lattice”).
cancel.g: To cross out something with lines etc.

candle.e: From Middle English candel, from Old English candel (“candle”), borrowed from Latin candēla (“candle”), from Latin candeō (“be white, bright, shining”, verb); see candid.
candle.g: A light source consisting of a wick embedded in a solid, flammable substance such as wax, tallow, or paraffin.

candlestick.e: From Middle English candelstik, candelstikke, from Old English candelsticca (“candlestick”), equivalent to candle + stick.
candlestick.g: A holder with a socket or spike for a candle.

cane.e: From Middle English cane, canne, from Old French cane (“sugar cane”), from Latin canna (“reed”), from Ancient Greek κάννα (kánna), from Akkadian 𒄀 (qanû, “reed”).
cane.g: A plant with simple stems, like bamboo or sugar cane, or the stem thereof:

canker.e: From Middle English canker, cancre, from Old English cancer (“cancer; crab”), akin to Dutch kanker, Old High German chanchar. Ultimately from Latin cancer (“a cancer”).
canker.g: A plant disease marked by gradual decay.

canker.e: From Middle English cankren, from the noun (see above).
canker.g: To affect as a canker; to eat away; to corrode; to consume.

cankered.e: From Middle English cancrede (preterite) and Middle English cankered, y-cancred (past participle) of Middle English cankren (“to canker”), equivalent to canker + -ed.

cankerworm.g: Either of two caterpillars, the larvae of geometrid moths, that are destructive to fruit, buds and leaves.

cannot.e: From Middle English can not, cannot, cannouȝt, etc. (compare Old English ne cann), equivalent to can + not.
cannot.g: Can not; be unable to (whether due to physical inability, logical impossibility, etc.).

canopy.e: From Middle English canapy, canepie, canapee, canape, canope, from Old French conopé, Medieval Latin canapeum, canopeum, from Latin cōnōpēum (“mosquito net, canopy”), from Ancient Greek κωνωπεῖον (kōnōpeîon, “mosquito net”), from Ancient Greek κώνωψ (kṓnōps, “mosquito”), of uncertain origin.
canopy.g: A high cover providing shelter, such as a cloth supported above an object, particularly over a bed.

capable.e: Borrowed from Middle French capable, from Late Latin capābilis.
capable.g: Able and efficient; having the ability needed for a specific task; having the disposition to do something; permitting or being susceptible t

capacity.e: From Middle English capacite, from Old French capacite, from Latin capācitās (whence -acity), from capāx (“able to hold much”), from capiō (“to hold, to contain, to take, to understand”).
capacity.g: The ability to hold, receive, or absorb.

cape.e: From Middle English cape, gappe, cap, from Old French cap (“cape, headland”), from Latin caput (“head”). For sense development, compare English ness (“a promontory point, cape”) from a root related to nose, Bulgarian нос (nos) (the same PIE root).
cape.g: A piece or point of land, extending beyond the adjacent coast into a sea or lake; a promontory; a headland.

cape.e: From French cape, from Old Occitan capa, from Late Latin cappa (“cape”). The second sense ("superhero") is metonymic from the fact that many superheroes wear capes. Likewise, the verb sense "defend, praise" alludes to the stereotypical depiction of superheroes wearing capes when they come to people's defense.
cape.g: A sleeveless garment or part of a garment, hanging from the neck over the back, arms, and shoulders.

caper.e: From Latin capparis, from Ancient Greek κάππαρις (kápparis).
caper.g: The pungent grayish green flower bud of the European and Oriental caper (Capparis spinosa), which is pickled and eaten.

capital.e: From Middle English capital, borrowed partly from Old French capital and partly from Latin capitālis (“of the head”) (in sense “head of cattle”), from caput (“head”) (English cap) + -ālis (suffix forming adjectives). Use in trade and finance originated in Medieval economies when a common but expensive transaction involved trading heads of cattle.
capital.g: Money and wealth: the means to acquire or produce goods and services, especially in a non-barter system.

capital.e: From Middle English capitale, partly from Old French capital and partly from Late Latin capitellum (“capital or chapiter of a column”), a form of Latin capitulum (“head-like object or structure; chapter”) (whence English capitulum, chapter, and the synonym chapiter (“uppermost part of a column”)), from caput (“head”) + -ulum (diminutive suffix).
capital.g: The uppermost part of a column.

capstone.e: From Middle English capston; equivalent to cap + stone.
capstone.g: Any of the stones making up the top layer of a wall; a coping stone.

captain.e: From Middle English capitain, capteyn, from Old French capitaine, from Late Latin capitāneus, from Latin caput (“head”) (English cap). Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kap-.

captivate.e: Borrowed from Late Latin captīvātus, the perfect passive participle of captīvō (“to capture”), from Latin captīvus (“captive, prisoner”) (ultimately from capiō (“to capture, seize”), from Proto-Indo-European *kap- (“to hold; to seize”)) + -ō (suffix forming first-conjugation verbs). Equivalent to captive + -ate (verb-forming suffix).
captivate.g: To make (a person, an animal, etc.) a captive; to take prisoner; to capture, to subdue.
Made captive; taken prisoner; captured, subdued.

captive.e: From Middle English captif; derived from Latin captīvus, probably through a borrowing from a Middle French intermediate. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kap- (“seize, hold”).
captive.g: One who has been captured or is otherwise confined.

captivity.e: From Middle English captivite, from Latin captīvitās. By surface analysis, captive + -ity. Entered into the English lexicon around the 14th century.

captor.e: Borrowed from Late Latin captor, from Latin capiō. English usage began around 1688.
captor.g: One who is holding a captive or captives.

capture.e: Borrowed from Middle French capture (noun), from Latin captūra.
capture.g: An act of capturing; a seizing by force or stratagem.

car.e: From Middle English carre, borrowed from Anglo-Norman carre, from Old Northern French (compare Old French char), from Latin carrus (“two-wheeled baggage wagon”), from Gaulish *karros, from Proto-Celtic *karros (“wagon”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱr̥sós (“vehicle”).
car.g: A wheeled vehicle that moves independently, with at least three wheels, powered mechanically, steered by a driver and mostly for personal tr

car.e: Acronym of contents of the address part of register number. Note that it was based on original hardware and has no meaning today.
car.g: The first part of a cons in Lisp. The first element of a list.

caravan.e: From Middle French caravane, from Old French carvane, from Persian کاروان (kârvân), from Middle Persian kʾlwʾn' (kārawān), from Old Persian 𐎣𐎠𐎼 (k-a-r, “people, subjects”). The word was used to designate a group of people who were travelling by camel or horse on the Silk Road.
caravan.g: A convoy or procession of travellers, their cargo and vehicles, and any pack animals, especially camels crossing a desert.

caraway.e: From Middle English caraway, carewey, carwey, from Medieval Latin carui, from Arabic كَرَاوِيَا (karāwiyā), via Aramaic from Ancient Greek καρώ (karṓ), κάρον (káron, “caraway”).
caraway.g: A biennial plant of species Carum carvi, native to Europe and Asia, mainly grown for its seed to be used as a culinary spice.

carbuncle.e: From Middle English carbuncle, charbocle, from Old French carbuncle, charbuncle, from Latin carbunculus (“a small coal; a reddish kind of precious stone; a kind of tumor”), diminutive of carbō (“a coal, charcoal”).
carbuncle.g: A deep-red or fiery colored garnet or other dark red precious stone, especially when cut cabochon.

carcass.e: Dated from the late 13th Century C.E.; from Anglo-Norman carcois, possibly related to Old French charcois. But cf. also Avestan 𐬐𐬀𐬵𐬭𐬐𐬁𐬯𐬀 (kahrkās, “vulture”), and Middle Persian (klkʾs /⁠kargās⁠/, “vulture”), whence Persian کرکس (karkas, “vulture”).
carcass.g: The body of a dead animal, especially a vertebrate or other animal having flesh.

care.e: From Middle English care, from Old English caru, ċearu (“care, concern, anxiety, sorrow, grief, trouble”), from Proto-West Germanic *karu, from Proto-Germanic *karō (“care, sorrow, cry”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵeh₂r- (“shout, call”). Related also to Dutch karig (“scanty”), German karg (“sparse, meagre, barren”), Latin garriō, Ancient Greek γῆρυς (gêrus).

From Middle English caren, carien, from Old English carian (“to sorrow, grieve, be troubled, be anxious, to care for, heed”), from Proto-West Germanic *karōn (“to care”), from Proto-Germanic *karōną (“to care”).
care.g: To be concerned (about), to have an interest (in); to feel concern (about).

careful.e: From Middle English careful, from Old English carful; equivalent to care + -ful.
careful.g: Taking care; attentive to potential danger, error or harm; cautious.

carefully.e: From Middle English carfulli, carefulliche, from Old English carfullīċe, ċearfullīċe (“carefully, diligently”), equivalent to careful + -ly.

carefulness.e: From Middle English, from Old English carfulnes (“care, anxiety, a charge, cure of souls, solicitude, carefulness, curiousness, curiosity”), equivalent to careful + -ness.

careless.e: From Middle English careles, from Old English carlēas (“careless, reckless, void of care, free from care, free”), equivalent to care + -less.

caress.e: From French caresse, from Italian carezza (“dear”), from Latin cārus (“dear”), from Proto-Indo-European *keh₂-, akin to Sanskrit काम (kāma, “love”).
caress.g: An act of endearment; any act or expression of affection; an embracing, or touching, with tenderness.

cargo.e: Borrowed from Spanish cargo (“load, burden”), from cargar (“to load”), from Late Latin carricō.
cargo.g: Freight carried by a ship, aircraft, or motor vehicle.

caring.e: From care + -ing. The adjective follows from the verb.

carnage.e: Borrowed from Middle French carnage, from a Norman or Picard variant Old Northern French) of Old French charnage, from char (“flesh”), or from Vulgar Latin *carnaticum (“slaughter of animals”), itself from Latin carnem, accusative of caro (“flesh”). By surface analysis, Latin carn- + -age.

carnal.e: From Middle English carnal, from Old French charnel, from Late Latin carnālis (“fleshy”), from oblique stem of Latin carō, carnis (“meat, flesh”) + -ālis (whence -al).
carnal.g: Relating to the physical and especially sexual appetites or activities.

carnelian.e: From cornelian, the red form named carneolus under the influence of Latin carneus (“fleshy”) because of its color.
carnelian.g: A hard, reddish brown chalcedony used in jewelry.

carouse.e: From Middle French carousser (“to quaff, drink, swill”), from German gar aus (literally “all out, quite out”), from gar austrinken (“to drink up entirely, guzzle”).
carouse.g: To engage in a noisy or drunken social gathering.

carouser.g: A person who carouses; a reveller.

carpenter.e: From Middle English carpenter, from Anglo-Norman carpenter (compare Old French charpentier), from Late Latin carpentārius (“a carpenter”), from Latin carpentārius (“a wagon-maker, carriage-maker”), from Latin carpentum (“a two-wheeled carriage, coach, or chariot, a cart”), from Gaulish carbantos.
carpenter.g: A person skilled at carpentry, the trade of cutting and joining timber in order to construct buildings or other structures.

carpet.e: From late Middle English carpette, from Old French carpite, from Medieval Latin carpita or Italian carpita, introduced in the 13th century by the Florentines from the Armenian Kingdom of Cilicia, from Middle Armenian կարպետ (karpet, “carpet, rug”), earlier կապերտ (kapert).
carpet.g: A fabric used as a complete floor covering.

carriage.e: From Middle English cariage, from Old Northern French cariage, from carier (“to carry”).

carrier.e: From Middle English cariere, partly from carien + -ere, after Anglo-Norman carier, cariour, and partly directly from Anglo-Norman. By surface analysis, carry + -er.
carrier.g: A person or object that carries someone or something else.

carry.e: From Middle English carien, from Anglo-Norman carier (modern French charrier); from a derivative of Latin carrus (“four-wheeled baggage wagon”), ultimately of Gaulish origin.
carry.g: To lift (something) and take it to another place; to transport (something) by lifting.

cart.e: From Middle English cart, kart, from Old Norse kartr (“wagon; cart”), merged with native Old English cræt (“a chariot; cart”), from Proto-Germanic *krattaz, *krattijô, *kradō, from Proto-Indo-European *gret- (“tracery; wattle; cradle; cage; basket”), from *ger- (“to turn, wind”). Wider cognates include Sanskrit ग्रन्थ (grantha, “a binding”).
cart.g: A small, open, wheeled vehicle, drawn or pushed by a person or animal, often with two wheels on one axle, more often used for transporting g
A tape cartridge used for pre-recorded material such as jingles and advertisements.

carve.e: From Middle English kerven, from Old English ceorfan, from Proto-West Germanic *kerban, from Proto-Germanic *kerbaną, from Proto-Indo-European *gerbʰ- (“to scratch”).

case.e: From Middle English cas, from Old French cas (“an event”), from Latin cāsus (“a falling, a fall; accident, event, occurrence; occasion, opportunity; noun case”), perfect passive participle of cadō (“to fall, to drop”).
case.g: An actual event, situation, or fact.

case.e: From Middle English case, from Old Northern French casse (compare Old French chasse (“box, chest, case”)), from Latin capsa (“box, bookcase”), from capiō (“to take, seize, hold”).
case.g: A box that contains or can contain a number of identical items of manufacture or commerce.

cask.g: A large barrel for the storage of liquid, especially of alcoholic drinks. (See a diagram of cask sizes.)

cassia.e: From Latin cassia (“cinnamon”), from Ancient Greek κασσία, κασία, κάσια (kassía, kasía, kásia), from Hebrew קְצִיעָה (qəṣīʿā), from Aramaic קְצִיעֲתָא (qəṣīʿătā), from קְצַע (qṣaʿ, “to cut off”).
cassia.g: The spice made from the bark of members of the genus Cinnamomum other than true cinnamon (C. verum), when they are distinguished from cinnam

cast.e: From Middle English casten, from Old Norse kasta (“to throw, cast, overturn”), from Proto-Germanic *kastōną (“to throw, cast”), of unknown origin. The senses relating to broadcasting are based on that same term; compare -cast.
cast.g: To move, or be moved, away.

casting.e: From Middle English castynge, castand, equivalent to cast + -ing.

castle.e: From Middle English castle, castel, from late Old English castel, castell (“a town, village”), borrowed from Late Latin castellum (“small camp, fort”), diminutive of Latin castrum (“camp, fort, citadel, stronghold”).
castle.g: A large residential building or compound that is fortified and contains many defences; in previous ages often inhabited by a nobleman or kin

catapult.e: From Middle French catapulte, from Latin catapulta, from Ancient Greek καταπέλτης (katapéltēs), from κατά (katá, “downwards, into, against”) + πάλλω (pállō, “to poise or sway a missile before it is thrown”).
catapult.g: A device or weapon for throwing or launching large objects.

catastrophe.e: From Ancient Greek καταστροφή (katastrophḗ), from καταστρέφω (katastréphō, “to overturn”), from κατά (katá, “down, against”) + στρέφω (stréphō, “to turn”).
catastrophe.g: Any large and disastrous event of great significance.

catch.e: From Middle English cacchen, from Anglo-Norman cachier, variant of Old French chacier, from Late Latin captiāre, from Latin captāre, frequentative of capere. Via PIE cognate with have. Middle English lacchen ("to catch" and heavily displaced Modern English latch), from Old English læċċan.
catch.g: The act of seizing or capturing.

cattle.e: From Middle English catel, from Anglo-Norman catel (“personal property”), from Old Northern French (compare French cheptel, Old French chetel, chatel, also English chattel) from Medieval Latin capitāle, from Latin capitālis (“of the head”) (whence also capital, from caput (“head”) + -alis (“-al”)). For the sense evolution, compare pecuniary and fee.
cattle.g: Domesticated animals of the species Bos taurus (cows, bulls, steers, oxen etc), and other hoofed mammals of the genus Bos.

caul.e: From Middle English calle, kelle, kalle, kolle (“caul, net, basket”), from Old English cāwl, cāul, cēawl, cēaul (“basket, container, net, sieve”), of uncertain origin. Reinforced by Old French cale (“close-fitting cap”), possibly a borrowing of the Old English term above, or alternatively related to Old French calotte (“headdress”).
caul.g: A style of close-fitting circular cap worn by women in the sixteenth century and later, often made of linen.

cauldron.e: From Middle English caudroun, borrowed from Old Northern French caudron, ultimately from Late Latin caldāria (“cooking-pot”), from Latin caldus (“hot”). Spelling later Latinized by having an l inserted. The military sense is a semantic loan from German Kessel; compare English kettling.
cauldron.g: A large bowl-shaped pot used for boiling over an open flame.

cause.e: From Middle English cause (also with the sense of “a thing”), borrowed from Old French cause (“a cause, a thing”), borrowed from Latin causa (“reason, sake, cause”), from Proto-Italic *kaussā, which is of unknown origin. From Middle English causen, Old French causer and Medieval Latin causāre.
cause.g: The source of, or reason for, an event or action; that which produces or effects a result.

causeless.e: From Middle English causelees, causeles; equivalent to cause + -less.
causeless.g: Having no obvious cause; fortuitous or inexplicable.

causeway.e: From Middle English cawcewey, with the first element from Middle English cauce, from Anglo-Norman, Old Northern French caucee or Old French caucie, cauchie (“route, highway”).
causeway.g: A road that is raised so as to be above water, marshland, and similar low-lying obstacles, which in some cases may flood periodically (e.g.

caution.e: Recorded since 1297 as Middle English caucioun (“bail, guarantee, pledge”), from Old French caution (“security, surety”), itself from Latin cautiō, from cautus, past participle of caveō, cavēre (“be on one's guard”).
caution.g: Prudence when faced with, or when expecting to face, danger; care taken in order to avoid risk or harm.

cautious.g: Using or exercising caution; careful; tentative

cavalry.e: From Middle French cavalerie, in turn from Italian cavalleria. Recorded in English from the 1540s.
cavalry.g: The military arm of service that fights while riding horses.

cave.e: From Middle English cave, borrowed from Old French cave, from Latin cava (“cavity”), from cavus (“hollow”).
cave.g: A large, naturally-occurring cavity formed underground or in the face of a cliff or a hillside.

cave.e: Borrowed from Latin cavē, second-person singular present active imperative of caveō (“to beware”). Used at Eton College, Berkshire.

cavern.e: From Middle English caverne, borrowing from Old French caverne, from Latin caverna (“hollow, cavity, cave”), from cavus (“hollow, excavated, concave”).

come.e: From Middle English comen, cumen, from Old English cuman, from Proto-West Germanic *kweman, from Proto-Germanic *kwemaną (“to come”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʷémt (“to step; to arrive”), from *gʷem- (“to come, step”).
come.g: To move nearer to the point of perspective.
